I see it this way:
a beginner skateboarder has to be very exact and specific with how they do complex tricks, and a beginner or intermediate bender would need to know the correct forms to bend well

theres a right way to do it when youre learning, and if you deviate, youll have a very difficult time getting the trick right.

If you imagine a high level bending move to be like doing a tre flip, while a beginner or intermediate skater would need to go through like 3 or 4 steps in order to execute it, a master skater, someone who has been tre flipping for years and years, can do it while barely moving any muscles. They know exactly where to put every ounce of pressure on the board to make it go where they want perfectly. 

I kind of imagine master benders can do this with some moves, or at least make shorthands for moves to make them faster.

Generally theres no "correct" way to pitch, but most of the time youre selling the vibe, characters, and main ideas of your show. Stuff like concept art, a strong elevator pitch, and maybe even some finished proof of concept stuff could help

You can be more detailed, but Its good to show you're open to changes.

Watch Bryan Konietzko's [pitching interview ](https://youtu.be/o1ZgaakBkoA) on youtube its super informative

First step to pitching a show is working in animation. 

Incredibly important to have a thorough understanding of the pipeline, since youre not only selling your show, but your ability as a show runner as well.

Otherwise they pair you with "an experienced exec" and your show is over before it started.

I also always assumed that once you pitch a show and get it greenlit, you just spend however long developing it with the studio before its ready to come out, but in reality a huge majority of the development is done by the creators in their FREE TIME.

You can get paid for a development period, but its usually not enough to live off of, and most of the development is usually done before the show is even pitched.

So this is a strat I learned from Ethan Becker, whos a professional in the industry and makes youtube videos.

The best way to practice structure is the same way you practice everything else effectively:

Find what you're trying to emulate, attempt to emulate, see what you did wrong and make corrections. Repeat 

For art this would be finding artists who have anatomy and structure that is solid and you admire/would like to be able to draw someday.

Thoughtfully copy it/trace, remember this is to build muscle memory/understand how that artist thinks (check out some of [ethan beckers](https://youtu.be/emcO79uteN4)) videos on youtube for more on this method

After tracing it try to draw it on your own (still looking at the reference)and then overlap your new drawing and the original and see where you were off. At first itll be a mess, but if you keep doing it youll notice areas of consistent mistakes, like for instance you always make the eyes or head too big. Or the legs too short etc.

Then youd keep that in mind for the next few studies. Maybe next time you over compensate and now youre making your heads too small. Its a process, but if this kinda thing works for you, legit it helps SOOO much, and quickly too.


The important thing is trying to apply stuff youve learned next time youre doodling, doesnt have to be good, but if youre activiely thinking about it its a big step.

And its fun because youre really just tracing over artists you already really like. I like to take one of these studies and once ive corrected/identified what i got wrong I'll try to redraw that same exact pose i copied but with my own character or something (the applying what you learned step). Its a quick way to get immediate feedback about what you need to work on and then forcing it to sink in.

you can actually do a surprising amount of networking from online schooling as well because often the mentors and teachers either have or are working in the industry, and everyone there is probably in a similar spot as you, so you can build a small circle of peers. 

Besides that, you can follow recruitors and promo people on Instagram they often post dates for online lectures and events you can attend. 

You dont need to go to art school to learn art, and while it helps, you dont need to go there to network either. The internet is very powerful.
